title: The Beginning of the Gospel
subtitle: Mark 1:1–13
description: No genealogy, no manger: Mark opens with Isaiah's voice, John at the Jordan, and Jesus driven into the wilderness.
paragraphs: Mark does not begin with a genealogy or a manger or a star. He begins like a man in a hurry, with a headline and an old voice. The headline is his whole book in one line: “This is the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.” The voice belongs to Isaiah the prophet, and it speaks before anything in the story has happened: “Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way.” Then the second line, the one that gives the messenger his shape: “A voice of one calling in the wilderness, ’Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him.’” Mark is telling you, before he shows you anything, that what comes next was announced centuries ahead of time, and that it starts out in the desert.

The messenger appears exactly where the voice said he would. John the Baptist comes preaching in the wilderness, and his message fits in a single phrase: “a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.” The whole region answers it. People stream out to him from all of Jerusalem and the countryside of Judea, confessing their sins as they come, and he baptizes them in the Jordan River. He looks like a prophet out of the old books, because he is meant to: “John was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist. His food was locusts and wild honey.” No city pulpit, no priestly robes. A man standing in a river at the edge of the wilderness, telling Israel to turn around.

And the moment the crowds gather, he points away from himself. “After me will come One more powerful than I,” he proclaims, “the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie.” Untying a man's sandals was a slave's work, the lowest task in the house, and John measures himself below it beside the One who is coming. Then he draws the line between his ministry and that One's: “I baptize you with water, but He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.” Water can wash skin and mark a turning. What the coming One brings is bigger than John's whole river, and John says so to the crowds standing in it.

Then Jesus comes up out of the crowd. Mark gives him no introduction beyond a hometown: “In those days Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan.” He has said nothing and done nothing yet in this Gospel, and he goes down into the water with the confessors. What happens next happens to him as he comes up: “As soon as Jesus came up out of the water, He saw the heavens breaking open and the Spirit descending on Him like a dove.” And over the breaking heavens a voice speaks the words the whole Gospel will spend itself testing: “You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.”

Mark wastes no time at all on what comes next; his favorite word is at once, and he spends it here. “At once the Spirit drove Jesus into the wilderness.” Not led, the way Matthew tells it. Driven. The same Spirit who rested on him like a dove now drives him out to meet the enemy before he has preached a sermon or called a disciple: “and He was there for forty days, being tempted by Satan.” Mark gives no dialogue, no stones, no pinnacle. He gives two facts and leaves them side by side: “He was with the wild animals, and the angels ministered to Him.” The beloved Son, fresh from the opened heavens, alone in the desert with the beasts and the tempter, and somehow also attended. That is where Mark's Gospel properly starts moving, and it does not slow down again.

title: Follow Me
subtitle: Mark 1:14–45
description: The kingdom sermon, four fishermen called mid-task, a synagogue amazed, and a leper whose news drives Jesus into the desert.
paragraphs: John's arrest is the hinge. Mark reports it in half a sentence and moves on: “After the arrest of John, Jesus went into Galilee and proclaimed the gospel of God.” The herald is in a cell, and the One he announced takes up the preaching himself, in the north country, far from the capital. His sermon is as short as John's and twice as large: “The time is fulfilled,” He said, “and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe in the gospel!” Everything Mark is about to show you flows out of that sentence. The time is fulfilled. The kingdom is near. The only response asked for is turning, and believing.

The first response comes from working men, and it costs them their living in a single breath. Walking beside the Sea of Galilee, Jesus sees Simon and his brother Andrew casting a net, and says the words that will empty boats all through this Gospel: “Come, follow Me,” Jesus said, “and I will make you fishers of men.” Mark does not record a pause, a question, or a negotiation. “And at once they left their nets and followed Him.” A little farther on, James and John are mending nets in their father's boat, and the same thing happens: “Immediately Jesus called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men and followed Him.” Four fishermen, one morning, no explanations. Mark's Jesus does not recruit. He calls, and men stand up out of their old lives mid-task.

What he does next explains why they followed. In Capernaum's synagogue on the Sabbath he teaches, and the room feels the difference before it can name it: “The people were astonished at His teaching, because He taught as one who had authority, and not as the scribes.” Then a man with an unclean spirit screams his name and his title in public: “I know who You are,” he cries, “the Holy One of God!” Jesus' first command to the spirit world in this Gospel is a muzzle: “Be silent!” He said. “Come out of him!” The spirit throws the man into convulsions, shrieks, and leaves, and the congregation asks the question the whole book will keep asking: “What is this? A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey Him!” Mark notes the result in one line: “And the news about Jesus spread quickly through the whole region of Galilee.”

That evening the synagogue becomes a sickroom. Simon's mother-in-law lies in bed with a fever, and Jesus takes her by the hand and lifts her up. “The fever left her, and she began to serve them.” After sunset, when the Sabbath rest ends, the whole town is at the door with its sick and its demon-possessed, and he heals and delivers until the house is emptied. Before dawn he is gone. “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up and went out to a solitary place to pray.” Simon hunts him down with the crowd's demand: “Everyone is looking for You!” And Jesus refuses the demand and chooses the road instead: “Let us go on to the neighboring towns so I can preach there as well, for that is why I have come.” Fame in one town is not the mission. On he goes, through Galilee, preaching and driving out demons.

The chapter ends with the exchange that undoes his secrecy. A leper kneels before him with a sentence that is almost a dare: “If You are willing, You can make me clean.” Jesus is “Moved with compassion,” and then he does the unthinkable thing for a holy man to do to an unclean one: he reaches out and touches him. “I am willing,” He said. “Be clean!” The leprosy leaves immediately, and Jesus sends the man off with a stern warning to tell no one and show himself to the priest. The man tells everyone instead. “Consequently, Jesus could no longer enter a town in plain view, but He stayed out in solitary places. Yet people came to Him from every quarter.” The cleansed man preaches, the preacher is driven to the desert, and the crowds come anyway. That is the pattern of the whole Gospel, set in its first chapter.

title: The Son of Man Has Authority on Earth
subtitle: Mark 2:1–3:6
description: A paralytic lowered through a roof, a tax collector called, the fasting question, and two Sabbaths that end in a murder plot.
paragraphs: The house in Capernaum is packed to the door when four men arrive carrying a fifth. Unable to get through, they climb up, uncover the roof, dig through it, and lower their friend on his mat into the room at Jesus' feet. Mark is careful about what Jesus notices first. It is not the hole in the roof or the interruption. “When Jesus saw their faith, He said to the paralytic, ‘Son, your sins are forgiven.’” The man came for his legs and gets his sins named first. Some scribes sitting there say nothing out loud, but their hearts say it for them: “Why does this man speak like this? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?” They have the theology right. Only God forgives sins. That is exactly the problem standing in front of them.

Jesus answers the unspoken charge with a question that turns the room into a courtroom. “Which is easier: to say to a paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up, pick up your mat, and walk’?” Forgiveness is the easier sentence to pronounce, because no one can check it. Walking is checkable on the spot. Then he states the claim the whole Gospel hangs on: “But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins...” He said to the paralytic, “I tell you, get up, pick up your mat, and go home.” The man gets up in front of them all, mat in hand, and walks out. “As a result, they were all astounded and glorified God, saying, ‘We have never seen anything like this!’” The invisible claim had been made visible, and the scribes' own test had proved it.

By the sea he calls a man the scribes would not be seen with. Levi son of Alphaeus is at the tax booth, a collector for Rome, when the same two words reach him: “Follow Me,” He told him, “and Levi got up and followed Him.” That evening Jesus is at Levi's table, and the guest list is the scandal: “many tax collectors and sinners were eating with Him and His disciples.” The scribes of the Pharisees go to the disciples with the obvious question: “Why does He eat with tax collectors and sinners?” Jesus answers it himself, and the answer is a mission statement: “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” In Mark, the table is a hospital ward, and the doctor eats with the patients.

Next comes the question of fasting. John's disciples fast; the Pharisees fast; Jesus' disciples are seen feasting, and people want to know why. His answer is a wedding: “How can the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them? As long as He is with them, they cannot fast.” Then, in the middle of the defense, the first shadow of the cross falls across this Gospel: “But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.” And the newness sayings follow like a warning label. “No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. If he does, the new piece will pull away from the old, and a worse tear will result.” “And no one pours new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the wine will burst the skins, and both the wine and the wineskins will be ruined.” What has arrived in him cannot be stapled onto the old arrangements. It will tear them.

The last two scenes run on the Sabbath, and they end in a plot. Walking through grainfields, his disciples pick heads of grain, and the Pharisees charge them with unlawful work. Jesus answers out of their own Scriptures, to David in the days of Abiathar the high priest, who “entered the house of God and ate the consecrated bread,” and then lays down the principle: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.” Days later, in a synagogue, a man with a withered hand is placed where everyone can watch what Jesus will do. “Which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?” The room will not answer. “Jesus looked around at them with anger and sorrow at their hardness of heart. Then He said to the man, ‘Stretch out your hand.’ So he stretched it out, and it was restored.” The response to mercy is a murder conference: “At this, the Pharisees went out and began plotting with the Herodians how they might kill Jesus.” Two chapters in, and the cross is already being arranged.

title: He Appointed Twelve
subtitle: Mark 3:7–35
description: Crowds at the sea, twelve names appointed, the Beelzebul charge answered, and the family of Jesus redrawn at a doorway.
paragraphs: Jesus withdraws to the sea, and half the map follows him. Mark lists the regions like a roll call: Galilee, Judea, “Jerusalem, Idumea, the region beyond the Jordan, and the vicinity of Tyre and Sidon.” The crowds press so hard to touch him that he has a boat kept ready “so that the crowd would not crush Him.” And the spirit world keeps blurting out what the human world has not yet figured out: “And when the unclean spirits saw Him, they fell down before Him and cried out, ‘You are the Son of God!’” His answer is the sternest hush in the Gospel so far: “But He warned them sternly not to make Him known.” The demons know his name. He will not let them announce it.

Out of the multitude he builds a small company. On a mountain he calls “those He wanted,” and appoints twelve “to accompany Him, to be sent out to preach, and to have authority to drive out demons.” Mark names them all, and the names carry their stories in advance. Simon gets a new name on the spot: “Simon (whom He named Peter).” James and John get a nickname that fits their tempers: “James son of Zebedee and his brother John (whom He named Boanerges, meaning ‘Sons of Thunder’).” And the list ends with the name that hangs over every later list: “and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus.” Mark does not wait for chapter 14 to tell you how one of the twelve ends. He writes the ending into the appointment.

The pressure gets to his own family before it gets to him. Back home the crowd is so thick that Jesus and his disciples cannot even eat, and his family comes to seize him, using the language of a mental collapse: “He is out of His mind.” At the same time the official verdict arrives from Jerusalem. The scribes who had come down deliver it in a sentence: “He is possessed by Beelzebul,” and, “By the prince of the demons He drives out demons.” It is the worst explanation available, and Jesus takes it apart with a parable and a picture. “How can Satan drive out Satan? If a kingdom is divided against itself, it cannot stand.” An exorcist who works for Satan would be burning down his own kingdom. The real explanation is the opposite one: “no one can enter a strong man’s house to steal his possessions unless he first ties up the strong man. Then he can plunder his house.” The demons are leaving because the house has a stronger occupant now, and he has been bound.

Then comes the warning that has unsettled readers ever since, and Mark tells you exactly what provoked it. “Truly I tell you, the sons of men will be forgiven all sins and blasphemies, as many as they utter. But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven; he is guilty of eternal sin.” Forgiveness is nearly total in this Gospel: all sins, as many blasphemies as they utter. The one unforgivable act is the one the scribes have just committed, and Mark names their crime in the next breath: “Jesus made this statement because they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit.’” They had looked at the Spirit's own work and filed it under Satan. That settled mislabeling, not a stray word, is the sin that cannot be unwound.

The episode ends with two families standing on either side of a door. Outside: “Then Jesus’ mother and brothers came and stood outside. They sent someone in to summon Him.” Inside: a crowd seated in a circle around him. Told who is waiting, he asks the question no devoted son is supposed to ask: “Who are My mother and My brothers?” Then he looks at the circle of listeners around him and redraws the family line through the middle of the room: “Here are My mother and My brothers! For whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother.” Mary is outside the door in this Gospel, with the brothers who think he has lost his mind. The family of Jesus, from here on, is defined by doing God's will, not by blood.

title: The Parables by the Sea
subtitle: Mark 4:1–34
description: The sower and the soils, the lamp, the seed growing while the farmer sleeps, and the smallest seed of all.
paragraphs: The crowd by the sea has grown so large that Jesus teaches from a boat, sitting on the water while the people stand along the shore. And the teaching, Mark says, comes in parables, beginning with the one that explains all the others. “Listen! A farmer went out to sow his seed.” Some falls along the path, “and the birds came and devoured it.” Some falls on rock, springs up fast, and scorches rootless in the sun. Some falls among thorns and is choked. “Still other seed fell on good soil, where it sprouted, grew up, and produced a crop,” and the yields run past all farming sense: “thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or a hundredfold.” Then the refrain that turns the story into a test of the hearers: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

Alone with the Twelve, Jesus tells them the parables are not a puzzle for outsiders but a dividing line. “The mystery of the kingdom of God has been given to you, but to those on the outside everything is expressed in parables.” Then he quotes Isaiah's bleak commission on the hardened: “they may be ever seeing but never perceiving, and ever hearing but never understanding; otherwise they might turn and be forgiven.” And he warns his own circle before he explains a word: “Do you not understand this parable? Then how will you understand any of the parables?” The explanation, when it comes, is about hearing itself. “The farmer sows the word.” The path is the hearer Satan robs at once. The rock is joy without root, gone at the first trouble. The thorns are the crowded heart, where “the worries of this life, the deceitfulness of wealth, and the desire for other things come in and choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful.” The good soil hears, receives, and bears. Four soils, one seed, and the difference is never the sowing.

The smaller sayings that follow press the same point from other sides. A lamp is not lit to be hidden: “Does anyone bring in a lamp to put it under a basket or under a bed? Doesn’t he set it on a stand?” What is hidden now will be disclosed; hearing is a measure that measures back: “With the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and even more will be added to you.” Then Mark gives a parable no other Gospel has, the seed growing secretly, and it is the quietest picture of the kingdom in the book. A man scatters seed and goes to bed. “Night and day he sleeps and wakes, and the seed sprouts and grows, though he knows not how.” “All by itself the earth produces a crop,” stalk, head, ripe grain, and the farmer's only real work is the harvest at the end. The kingdom grows while its servants sleep, by a life they did not invent and cannot hurry.

Last comes the smallest seed of all. “It is like a mustard seed, which is the smallest of all seeds sown upon the earth.” Planted, “it grows to be the largest of all garden plants and puts forth great branches, so that the birds of the air nest in its shade.” From the least beginning, a tree big enough to shelter the birds of heaven. That is the chapter's whole argument about the kingdom: it starts beneath notice and ends beyond calculation, and the soils, the lamp, the sleeping farmer, and the mustard seed are all saying it. Mark closes the teaching day with the method itself: “With many such parables Jesus spoke the word to them, to the extent that they could understand. He did not tell them anything without using a parable. But privately He explained everything to His own disciples.”

title: Peace, Be Still
subtitle: Mark 4:35–5:43
description: A storm stilled, a legion sent into the sea, a woman healed by a touch, and a twelve-year-old raised with two Aramaic words.
paragraphs: That same evening he says, “Let us cross to the other side,” and the parable teacher is carried into a storm. The waves break over the boat until it is swamping, and Jesus is in the stern asleep on the cushion. The disciples wake him with the most human prayer in the Gospel: “Teacher, don’t You care that we are perishing?” He gets up and speaks to the weather the way he spoke to the demon in the synagogue: “Silence!” He commanded. “Be still!” The wind dies and the sea goes perfectly calm. Then the rebuke turns around: “Why are you so afraid?” He asked. “Do you still have no faith?” The men are more frightened after the calm than during the storm: “Overwhelmed with fear, they asked one another, ‘Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?’”

On the far shore, in the region of the Gerasenes, the storm is waiting on land. A man from the tombs meets the boat, a man no chain could hold, who “kept crying out and cutting himself with stones” night and day among the graves. He runs and falls on his knees, and the voice that comes out of him knows exactly who has landed: “What do You want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg You before God not to torture me!” Asked his name, he answers for a crowd: “My name is Legion,” he replied, “for we are many.” The legion begs its way into a herd of pigs on the hillside, and “the herd of about two thousand rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the water.” The herdsmen run to town with the news, and the townspeople come out and find the wild man “sitting there, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid.” Their verdict on the miracle is a request: they beg Jesus to leave their region.

The freed man begs the opposite, to go with him, and gets the one commission in this Gospel given to a Gentile. “Go home to your own people,” He said, “and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and what mercy He has shown you.” So the man who was sent away from Jesus becomes his herald through the Decapolis, and everyone is amazed. Back across the sea, the pattern reverses: a synagogue leader named Jairus falls at Jesus' feet with a father's plea: “My little daughter is near death. Please come and place Your hands on her, so that she will be healed and live.” On the way, in the pressing crowd, a woman who has bled for twelve years and spent everything on doctors reaches from behind and touches his cloak, saying what she has evidently been saying to herself: “If only I touch His garments, I will be healed.” The bleeding stops at once, and Jesus stops too, aware that power has gone out of him, asking who touched him.

She comes forward trembling and tells him the whole truth, and he gives her the name no one else gets in this Gospel: “Daughter,” said Jesus, “your faith has healed you. Go in peace and be free of your affliction.” While he is still speaking, the messengers arrive with the news the delay has cost: Jairus' daughter is dead. Jesus answers the father before the grief can settle: “Do not be afraid; just believe.” At the house, over the professional mourners' noise, he says the sentence they laugh at: “Why all this commotion and weeping? The child is not dead, but asleep.” He puts them all outside, takes the parents and the three, and takes the girl by the hand: “Talitha koum!” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, get up!” She gets up and walks around, twelve years old, and the house is astounded. His last instructions are a strict order of silence, and something to eat for the girl. In one chapter the sea obeys him, a legion leaves a man, a woman's faith stops twelve years of bleeding, and death itself is treated as a sleep he can wake a child from.

title: A Prophet Without Honor
subtitle: Mark 6:1–29
description: Nazareth takes offense, the Twelve are sent out with a staff, and Herod's banquet ends with the Baptist's head on a platter.
paragraphs: At home it falls apart. In Nazareth's synagogue the teaching that astonished Capernaum produces only a familiarity that curdles. “Where did this man get these ideas?” they asked. “What is this wisdom He has been given? And how can He perform such miracles?” Then the local knowledge comes out like an indictment: “Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and the brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? Aren’t His sisters here with us as well?” They know his trade, his mother, his brothers by name, his sisters in the room, and the knowing is itself the obstacle. “And they took offense at Him.”

His answer is a proverb about hometowns: “Only in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own household is a prophet without honor.” And Mark records the strangest limitation in the Gospel: “So He could not perform any miracles there, except to lay His hands on a few of the sick and heal them.” Unbelief does not merely refuse the gift; somehow it restricts the giver. “And He was amazed at their unbelief.” The man who was amazed at nothing else in this Gospel, not storms or legions, stands amazed at the closed door of his own town. He leaves, teaching from village to village, and sends the Twelve out in pairs with almost nothing: a staff, sandals, no bread, no bag, no money, no second tunic. Their whole equipment is dependence. Where a house receives them, they stay; where it will not, they are to “shake the dust off your feet when you leave that place, as a testimony against them.” They go, and preach repentance, and drive out demons, and heal the sick with oil.

Their preaching reaches a palace, and Mark uses it to tell the story he has been holding back. King Herod hears the reports and reaches the conclusion of a guilty conscience: “John, whom I beheaded, has risen from the dead!” Then the flashback. Herod had arrested John for Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, because John kept saying the sentence that prophets die for: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife!” Herodias held the grudge and wanted him dead, but Herod stood in her way, of all people, because he “feared John and protected him, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man.” The king who jailed the prophet also shielded him, perplexed by his words, “yet he listened to him gladly.” It is the most divided portrait of a ruler in the Gospels: a man who loved to hear the voice he could not obey.

Herodias waits for a birthday. At the banquet for Galilee's great men, her daughter dances, the king is pleased past all judgment, and he swears in front of his guests: “Whatever you ask of me, I will give you, up to half my kingdom!” The girl goes out to her mother with the only question that matters: “What should I request?” The answer has been waiting for its moment for months: “The head of John the Baptist.” She hurries back and improves on it: “I want you to give me the head of John the Baptist on a platter immediately.” Mark says the king “was consumed with sorrow, but because of his oaths and his guests, he did not want to refuse her.” An executioner goes down to the prison, and the head of the voice in the wilderness is carried into a banquet on a dish, handed to a girl, who gives it to her mother. “When John’s disciples heard about this, they came and took his body and placed it in a tomb.” The forerunner's story ends with a burial, quietly, the way another story in this Gospel will end.

title: They Ate and Were Satisfied
subtitle: Mark 6:30–56
description: Five loaves feed five thousand, Jesus walks on the sea past his own disciples, and a whole region begs for the fringe of his cloak.
paragraphs: The apostles come back from their first mission with their reports, and Jesus tries to give them a rest. “Come with Me privately to a solitary place, and let us rest for a while.” The crowds have been so constant that they have not even had time to eat. The retreat lasts one boat ride. The crowd spots the departure, runs around the shore on foot, and is waiting on the far side when the boat lands. Jesus steps ashore, sees them, and Mark gives you the inside of the moment: “He had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd.” The shepherdless sheep get a sermon first: “And He began to teach them many things.”

By evening the disciples do the arithmetic and present the obvious solution: send them away to buy food. Jesus hands the arithmetic back: “You give them something to eat.” Their protest is a budget: should they spend two hundred denarii on bread for this? His question is an inventory: “Go and see how many loaves you have.” The count comes back at five loaves and two fish, against five thousand men. He seats the crowd in companies on the green grass, hundreds and fifties, like an army or a flock, takes the loaves and fish, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives, and the food passes through the disciples' hands to everyone. The result is three short clauses that climb: “They all ate and were satisfied,” and the fragments alone fill “twelve basketfuls of broken pieces of bread and fish.” Five loaves in, twelve baskets of leftovers out, and five thousand men fed in a desolate place.

Immediately he puts the disciples in the boat for Bethsaida and goes up the mountain alone to pray, and the night turns against them. In the fourth watch he sees them straining at the oars against the wind and comes to them walking on the sea, and Mark adds the eerie detail that “He intended to pass by them.” They see him and scream, certain it is a ghost. His answer is three short sentences that carry the whole Gospel's comfort: “Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.” He climbs in, the wind stops, and the disciples are utterly astounded, and Mark tells you why their astonishment is really a failure: “for they had not understood about the loaves, but their hearts had been hardened.” Hours after handing out the bread themselves, they meet the bread-giver on the water and do not know him.

The crossing ends at Gennesaret, and the rest is a montage of running. The people recognize him, and the whole region turns into stretcher-bearers, “carrying the sick on mats to wherever they heard He was.” Villages, towns, countryside, marketplaces: wherever he goes, the sick are laid out along his path, and the crowds beg for the smallest contact available: “just to let them touch the fringe of His cloak.” The sentence that ends the chapter has no exceptions in it: “And all who touched Him were healed.” The woman with the bleeding had found the way in the last episode, by faith and trembling. Now a whole countryside copies her, fringe by fringe.

title: Their Hearts Are Far from Me
subtitle: Mark 7:1–37
description: Tradition against commandment, a Syrophoenician mother who will not leave empty, and a deaf man's ears opened with a sigh.
paragraphs: The delegation from Jerusalem opens with a question about dishwashing. They have watched Jesus' disciples eat with unwashed hands, against the tradition of the elders, and they want an explanation. Jesus gives them Isaiah instead: “These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me. They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine the precepts of men.” Then the charge in his own words: “You have disregarded the commandment of God to keep the tradition of men.” And he proves it with their own loophole. Moses said to honor father and mother, but a man can declare his assets “Whatever you would have received from me is Corban,” a gift devoted to God, and be excused from supporting his parents for life. Religion itself has become the exemption from religion's central duty: “Thus you nullify the word of God by the tradition you have handed down. And you do so in many such matters.”

Then he calls the crowd back, every listener, and makes the announcement that rearranges the whole purity system: “Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him; but the things that come out of a man, these are what defile him.” Defilement does not travel inward from food or hands. It travels outward, from the heart. Inside the house the disciples ask about it, and his patience is thin: “Are you still so dull?” Food passes through the stomach and out; it never reaches the heart at all. Mark inserts, for his readers, the quiet bombshell in a parenthesis of his own: “(Thus all foods are clean.)” What defiles is the catalogue that comes out: “For from within the hearts of men come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, debauchery, envy, slander, arrogance, and foolishness.” “All these evils come from within, and these are what defile a man.”

He leaves Jewish territory entirely then, for Tyre, hoping for obscurity and not getting it. A Greek woman, a Syrophoenician, falls at his feet over a demon in her little daughter, and Jesus says the hardest sentence he says to any seeker in this Gospel: “First let the children have their fill,” He said. “For it is not right to take the children’s bread and toss it to the dogs.” She does not argue the insult away. She builds on it: “Yes, Lord,” she replied, “even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” It is the only time in Mark that someone wins an exchange with Jesus, and he rewards the answer on the spot: “Because of this answer, you may go. The demon has left your daughter.” She goes home and finds the child on the bed and the demon gone. A Gentile mother, told she is outside the children's table, believes there are crumbs enough for her house, and there are.

Back toward the sea, in the Decapolis, they bring him a man deaf and nearly mute, and Jesus takes him aside from the crowd alone. The healing is physical in a way this Gospel rarely lingers on: fingers in the man's ears, spittle on his tongue, a look up to heaven, and a deep sigh. Then the word, kept in its own language: Ephphatha, which means, “Be opened!” Ears open, tongue loosens, speech comes plain. Jesus orders silence about it, as always, and as always it fails in the opposite direction: the more he ordered them, the more widely they proclaimed it. The witnesses sum up the whole middle of Mark in one sentence of astonishment: “He has done all things well! He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!”

title: Beware the Leaven
subtitle: Mark 8:1–26
description: A second feeding, a refused sign, a boat full of men who cannot do the arithmetic, and a blind man healed in two stages.
paragraphs: Once again a crowd, once again nothing to eat, and this time Jesus raises the problem himself. “I have compassion for this crowd, because they have already been with Me three days and have nothing to eat.” They have followed him three days into a desolate place, some from a great distance, and sending them home hungry means watching them faint on the road. The disciples answer as if the last feeding had happened to someone else: “Where in this desolate place could anyone find enough bread to feed all these people?” The inventory is seven loaves and a few small fish. He seats the crowd on the ground, gives thanks, breaks, distributes, and Mark repeats the earlier result almost word for word, because the repetition is the lesson: “The people ate and were satisfied,” and the broken pieces left over fill seven baskets. About four thousand people. A second feeding, in Gentile country this time, and the disciples watched the same hands do it again.

The Pharisees come next, arguing, testing, demanding “a sign from heaven.” His answer is a sigh and a refusal with the door shut: “Why does this generation demand a sign? Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.” He leaves them standing there, gets back in the boat, and crosses. In the boat the disciples discover they have brought one loaf and fall into a worried conference about bread. Jesus, who has twice multiplied it in front of them, warns them about a different kind of bread entirely: “Watch out!” He cautioned them. “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod.” They hear bread. He means the slow, spreading corruption of men who demand signs and kings who kill prophets, and the misunderstanding opens the whole failure of the Twelve so far.

His rebuke comes as a catechism they cannot pass. “Why are you debating about having no bread? Do you still not see or understand? Do you have such hard hearts? ‘Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear?’ And do you not remember?” Then the arithmetic of memory, question by question. When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many basketfuls did you collect? “Twelve,” they answered. And the seven loaves for the four thousand? “Seven,” they said. They can recite every number and miss every meaning. The exchange ends on the question the whole Gospel has been building toward, asked this time of the insiders: “Do you still not understand?”

At Bethsaida the answer arrives as a picture. They bring a blind man, and Jesus leads him by the hand out of the village, spits on his eyes, lays his hands on him, and asks, “Can you see anything?” The man looks up with the most honest sentence in Mark: “I can see the people, but they look like trees walking around.” Sight has come, but only halfway: shapes without faces, people like trees. Jesus lays his hands on the man's eyes a second time, and “when he opened them his sight was restored, and he could see everything clearly.” It is the only gradual miracle in the Gospels, and Mark places it here, at the hinge of his book, like a parable in action. The disciples have seen the loaves, the sea, the demons, and they still see men like trees walking. Their blindness, like this man's, will take a second touch. He sends the man home with a boundary: “Do not go back into the village.”

title: He Began to Teach Them
subtitle: Mark 8:27–9:13
description: Peter confesses the Christ and rebukes him in the same hour, the cross is named a follower's road, and glory breaks out on a mountain.
paragraphs: On the road to the villages around Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks the question the whole first half of the Gospel has been circling. “Who do people say I am?” The answers are the public's best guesses: John the Baptist back from the dead, Elijah, one of the prophets. Then he closes the distance: “But what about you?” Jesus asked. “Who do you say I am?” Peter answers for them all, and it is the first time a human being in Mark says it plainly: “You are the Christ.” Jesus' response is not celebration but another stern silence, and then, immediately, the teaching that redefines the title: he begins “to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and that He must be killed and after three days rise again.” He speaks it, Mark says, quite frankly. No parable. The Christ is going to be killed.

Peter, who has just made the great confession, takes him aside to rebuke him for it, and the rebuke he gets back is the sharpest sentence Jesus speaks to a disciple in any Gospel: “Get behind Me, Satan! For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men.” The confessor of one minute is Satan in the next, because a Christ who will not suffer is the devil's Christ, not God's. Then Jesus calls the crowd in to hear what following such a Christ costs: “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me.” The cross is introduced in Mark not first as Jesus' fate but as his followers' wardrobe. “For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake and for the gospel will save it.” “What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his soul?”

Six days later, three of them see the glory that stands behind the suffering. On a high mountain, alone with Peter, James, and John, Jesus is transfigured: his clothes become “radiantly white, brighter than any launderer on earth could bleach them,” and Moses and Elijah appear, talking with him. Peter, terrified and out of ideas, offers construction: “Rabbi, it is good for us to be here.” Then the cloud comes, and the voice that spoke at the Jordan speaks again, this time to the disciples: “This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!” Suddenly they look around and see no one but Jesus. The law and the prophets step back, and the command that remains is hearing: listen to him, including what he has just said about suffering, which they have no intention of believing.

Coming down, he orders silence “until the Son of Man had risen from the dead,” and they obey the words while missing the meaning entirely, “discussing what it meant to rise from the dead.” Their question down the mountain is about Elijah, who was supposed to come first. His answer turns the prophecy into a gravestone: “But I tell you that Elijah has indeed come, and they have done to him whatever they wished, just as it is written about him.” Elijah has come, in John, and the forerunner's fate was prison and a platter. If that is what they did to the one who prepared the way, the disciples might have asked themselves what awaits the One whose way he prepared. Mark leaves the question hanging in the mountain air as they descend to a crowd, an argument, and a boy the other nine could not heal.

title: If Anyone Wants to Be First
subtitle: Mark 9:14–50
description: A father's honest prayer, a second prediction nobody understands, an argument about greatness, and a child set in the middle.
paragraphs: At the foot of the mountain the other nine are surrounded by a crowd, scribes arguing, and a failure. A father has brought his son, seized by a spirit that makes him mute, throws him down, foams, gnashes, rigid: “I asked Your disciples to drive it out, but they were unable.” Jesus' answer is aimed at the whole scene: “O unbelieving generation!” Jesus replied. “How long must I remain with you? How long must I put up with you? Bring the boy to Me.” The spirit convulses the boy at the sight of him. The father's plea is the most honest prayer in the Gospel, hedged and desperate at once: “But if You can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.” Jesus throws the hedge back at him: “If You can?” echoed Jesus. “All things are possible to him who believes!” And the father cries out the sentence believers have prayed ever since: “I do believe; help my unbelief!”

The command ends it: “You deaf and mute spirit,” He said, “I command you to come out and never enter him again.” The spirit shrieks, convulses the boy violently, and leaves him so still that the crowd says he is dead. Jesus takes him by the hand and lifts him up, the same gesture as with Jairus' daughter, and the boy stands. Later, in the house, the nine ask the professional question: “Why couldn’t we drive it out?” His answer prices their failure in one line: “This kind cannot come out, except by prayer.” Authority given is not authority owned; some victories only come to men who have been asking God instead of assuming.

Passing secretly through Galilee, he teaches the second passion prediction, plain as the first: “The Son of Man will be delivered into the hands of men. They will kill Him, and after three days He will rise.” Mark's comment on the class is four words deep: they did not understand, and they were afraid to ask. What they discuss instead, on the road behind him, is which of them is the greatest. In the house at Capernaum he asks what the argument was about, and the silence is total. Then he sits down, calls the Twelve formally to order, and overturns the ladder they have been climbing: “If anyone wants to be first, he must be the last of all and the servant of all.” He sets a little child in the middle of them, takes the child in his arms, and makes the child the measure of the kingdom's reception desk: “Whoever welcomes one of these little children in My name welcomes Me, and whoever welcomes Me welcomes not only Me, but the One who sent Me.”

John tries to change the subject to a boundary dispute: they have stopped a man casting out demons in Jesus' name because he was not one of the company. Jesus refuses the franchise: “Do not stop him,” Jesus replied. “For whoever is not against us is for us.” Then the tone darkens into the severest teaching in Mark, all of it aimed at the strong on behalf of the small. Causing a little one to stumble earns the millstone: better “to have a large millstone hung around his neck and to be thrown into the sea.” Hand, foot, eye, whatever in you causes sin gets the surgeon's sentence, because entering life maimed beats entering hell whole. And the teaching lands, of all places, on peace inside the little company that has spent the day arguing rank: “Have salt among yourselves, and be at peace with one another.” First, last, servant, child, outsider, millstone, salt. The road to Jerusalem is becoming a school, and the pupils are failing upward.

title: Let the Children Come to Me
subtitle: Mark 10:1–52
description: Marriage from Eden, children blessed, a rich man who goes away sad, thrones requested, and Bartimaeus who follows on the road.
paragraphs: The road south runs through a test. Pharisees ask whether a man may divorce his wife, and Jesus takes the question behind Moses to creation. Moses permitted the certificate, he says, “because of your hardness of heart.” But at the beginning God made them “male and female,” and the man leaves his parents and the two become one flesh. His conclusion is a sentence with no loopholes: “Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate.” In the house the disciples ask again, and he closes the private door too: “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery against her.” Mark adds the mirror case Matthew's audience would not have imagined, a wife divorcing a husband, under the same verdict. The standard is not the law's permission. It is Eden's design.

Then the disciples, fresh from greatness arguments, try to manage his schedule by shooing away people bringing little children for a blessing. This time Jesus is not patient: Mark says he was indignant. “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.” And the truth under the blessing is aimed at every adult in earshot: “Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.” The kingdom is not achieved like the rich man's record or climbed like the brothers' ladder. It is received, the way a child receives, empty-handed. “And He took the children in His arms, placed His hands on them, and blessed them.”

A man runs up and kneels with the chapter's great question: “Good Teacher,” he asked, “what must I do to inherit eternal life?” Jesus first questions the adjective: “Why do you call Me good?” Jesus replied. “No one is good except God alone.” The man recites his record, commandments kept from his youth, and Mark gives the most tender stage direction in the Gospel: Jesus looked at him and loved him. Then the loving sentence that ends the interview: “There is one thing you lack: Go, sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.” The man goes away in sorrow, because he had great wealth. Jesus turns to the disciples with the image no one forgets: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.” Their astonishment asks the real question, “Who then can be saved?” and his answer moves the whole matter out of human reach: “With man this is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.”

The road climbs toward Jerusalem, and for the third time he tells them the end of it, now with the details filled in: the Son of Man “will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes,” and the Gentiles “will mock Him and spit on Him and flog Him and kill Him. And after three days He will rise again.” Walking ahead of them alone, with the disciples amazed and the followers afraid, he hears Peter's bookkeeping: we have left everything. His answer promises the strangest economics in the Gospel, a hundredfold “in the present age” for anyone who has left home and fields “for My sake and for the gospel,” persecutions included in the dividend, “and in the age to come, eternal life.” Then the reversal that governs the whole road: “But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.”

The last two scenes prove it in opposite directions. James and John, the Sons of Thunder, ask for the thrones at his right and left in his glory, and the ten are indignant when they hear of it. Jesus gathers them and draws the line between the world's greatness and his: “But it shall not be this way among you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all.” Then he grounds it in himself, in the sentence that sums up Mark: “For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.” Out of Jericho, a blind beggar the crowd tries to hush will not be hushed: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” Jesus stops. “What do you want Me to do for you?” Jesus asked. “Rabboni,” said the blind man, “let me see again.” “Go,” said Jesus, “your faith has healed you.” Bartimaeus receives his sight and does the thing the rich man would not and the brothers only schemed at: he follows Jesus along the road.

title: He Found Nothing but Leaves
subtitle: Mark 11:1–33
description: A colt, a cheering crowd, a fruitless fig tree, a temple cleared, and a question about authority answered with a question.
paragraphs: The entry into Jerusalem is staged like a coronation by a king who chooses his own props. From Bethphage he sends two disciples for a colt “on which no one has ever sat,” with a password for anyone who challenges them: the Lord needs it. Cloaks go over the colt and under it, branches are cut and spread, and the procession shouts the psalm and adds a hope of its own: “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David!” He rides into the city, enters the temple courts, and Mark's account of the triumphal entry ends in the least triumphal way imaginable: he looked around at everything, saw it was late, and went back out to Bethany with the Twelve. The king inspects his capital and says nothing. The verdict waits until morning.

On the way in next day he is hungry, and a fig tree in leaf draws him: leafy trees promise early fruit. “But when He reached it, He found nothing on it except leaves, since it was not the season for figs.” His response startles everyone who hears it: “May no one ever eat of your fruit again.” A curse on a tree, out of season, for having leaves without fruit. The disciples hear the statement, Mark says, and the sentence hangs there while Jesus continues into the city and into the temple, where the same diagnosis is waiting in human form: a house full of religious leaf and no fruit. He drives out the buyers and sellers, overturns the money changers' tables and the dove sellers' seats, and stops the traffic using the courts as a shortcut. His charge joins two prophets in one breath: “Is it not written: ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it ‘a den of robbers.’”

The chief priests and scribes hear it and begin looking for a way to kill him, held back only by fear of the crowd astonished at his teaching. In the morning, walking back into the city, the disciples see the fig tree again: withered from the roots. Peter remembers out loud: “Look, Rabbi! The fig tree You cursed has withered.” Jesus answers the wonder with a lesson on prayer that treats the curse as an object lesson: “Have faith in God,” Jesus said to them. “Truly I tell you that if anyone says to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ and has no doubt in his heart but believes that it will happen, it will be done for him.” And attached to the promise, a condition this Gospel never lets prayer escape: “if you hold anything against another, forgive it, so that your Father in heaven will forgive your trespasses as well.” The tree was never really about the tree. It was about a temple with leaves, and about what God does with profession that bears nothing.

The authorities come at him in the courts with the question of credentials: “By what authority are You doing these things?” He offers a trade: answer his question and he will answer theirs. The question is a trap with two teeth: John's baptism, was it from heaven or from men? They deliberate where he can watch them do it. From heaven invites, why then did you not believe him? From men invites the crowd, who hold John a prophet, down on their heads. The guardians of Israel's truth choose the safest sentence available to them: “We do not know.” It earns them exactly what their dishonesty purchased: “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.” The interrogators leave with nothing, and the man without credentials keeps the temple.

title: The Stone the Builders Rejected
subtitle: Mark 12:1–44
description: Tenants who kill the son, Caesar's coin, a resurrection riddle undone, the greatest commandment, and a widow's two coins.
paragraphs: In the temple he tells a story everyone in the courtyard can decode. A man plants a vineyard, walls it, digs a wine vat, builds a tower, rents it to tenants, and goes away. At harvest he sends servant after servant for his share of the fruit, and the tenants beat one, strike one on the head, kill another, and work through the whole staff. Last of all he sends his beloved son, reasoning that they will respect him. The tenants reason differently: “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.” They seize the son, kill him, and throw his body out of the vineyard. Jesus asks his hearers to pronounce the sentence themselves, then answers it and seals it with the psalm: “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes.” The leaders understand the parable perfectly. That is the problem. They want to arrest him on the spot and are stopped only by fear of the crowd.

The traps that follow come dressed as compliments. Pharisees and Herodians, enemies yoked together for the purpose, open with flattery about his honesty and ask the question designed to impale him either way: “Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?” He asks for the coin, makes them produce Caesar's image from their own pockets, and asks whose it is. “Caesar’s,” they answered. “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” They marvel and have nothing. Then the Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, bring their riddle of seven brothers and one widow, expecting the doctrine to collapse into absurdity. He tells them the error is upstream of the riddle: “Aren’t you mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God?” In the resurrection “they will neither marry nor be given in marriage. Instead, they will be like the angels in heaven.” And from the burning bush he proves the premise they thought was safe: God named himself “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” to a Moses centuries after all three were buried. “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living. You are badly mistaken!”

Then a scribe comes who is not setting a trap, and the longest answer of the day is a gift. Asked which commandment stands first, Jesus recites Israel's creed and its consequence: “Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One. Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.” “The second is this: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ No other commandment is greater than these.” The scribe agrees, ranks love above every burnt offering, and hears the nearest thing to a compliment Jesus gives a scholar in this Gospel: “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” After that, Mark notes, no one dared question him any further.

He ends the day asking the questions himself. How can the scribes call the Christ David's son, when David, speaking by the Holy Spirit, calls him Lord? “David himself calls Him ‘Lord.’ So how can He be David’s son?” The crowd listens with delight. Then the warning against the scholars' theater, the long robes and the chief seats and the lengthy prayers, with its ugliest charge tucked inside: “They defraud widows of their houses, and for a show make lengthy prayers. These men will receive greater condemnation.” And as if to prove the point by contrast, he sits down opposite the treasury and watches the offerings until a poor widow puts in two small copper coins. He calls the disciples over for the last lesson of the day: “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put more than all the others into the treasury. For they all contributed out of their surplus, but she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on.”

title: Keep Watch
subtitle: Mark 13:1–37
description: The temple doomed, wars and witness, the abomination of desolation, the Son of Man coming in clouds, and a doorkeeper told to stay awake.
paragraphs: A disciple plays tour guide on the way out: “Teacher, look at the magnificent stones and buildings!” Jesus answers with the sentence that empties the whole complex: “Do you see all these great buildings?” Jesus replied. “Not one stone here will be left on another; every one will be thrown down.” On the Mount of Olives, opposite the temple, four of them, Peter, James, John, and Andrew, ask privately when it will happen and what sign will announce it. The discourse he gives them is less a timetable than a discipline, and its first word is a warning about deception itself: “See to it that no one deceives you.” Many will come in his name claiming to be him. Wars and rumors of wars will sound like the end and are not: “When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. These things must happen, but the end is still to come.” Earthquakes, famines, nation against nation: “These are the beginning of birth pains.”

What comes first for them is not escape but witness. They will be handed to councils, beaten in synagogues, and made to stand before governors and kings as testimony, and Mark sets the mission inside the persecution: “And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all the nations.” For the trials themselves they are told to leave their speeches unwritten: “do not worry beforehand what to say. Instead, speak whatever you are given at that time, for it will not be you speaking, but the Holy Spirit.” Families will split down the middle, brother betraying brother, children rising against parents, and the promise attached to the hatred is endurance, not rescue: “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

Then the crisis itself: “the abomination of desolation standing where it should not be,” with Mark's own whisper to whoever reads the book: let the reader understand. The instruction is flight without luggage: no one on the housetop goes back inside, no one in the field returns for his cloak, and woe to the pregnant and the nursing in those days. Pray it does not come in winter. “For those will be days of tribulation unseen from the beginning of God’s creation until now, and never to be seen again.” The only comfort inside the horror is a limit God himself sets: “If the Lord had not cut short those days, nobody would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, whom He has chosen, He has cut them short.” False Christs in that hour will work signs and wonders aimed at the elect themselves, and the defense is memory: “I have told you everything in advance.”

After the tribulation, the sky itself gives way, and the center of the chapter arrives. “At that time they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory.” The angels go out to gather the elect from the four winds, from the ends of earth to the ends of heaven. The fig tree, withered in chapter 11 and tender in spring, becomes the reading lesson: when you see these things, he is near, at the door. “Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.” And then the limit that keeps every generation honest, spoken by the Son about himself: “No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.”

So the discourse ends where it began, on watchfulness, now pictured as a house at night. A master goes on a journey, gives each servant his task, and charges the doorkeeper to stay awake, because the return may fall in any watch of the night: evening, midnight, rooster crow, morning. To be found sleeping is the only failure the parable names. The last line widens the audience past the four on the mountain to whoever has ever read the page: “And what I say to you, I say to everyone: Keep watch!” Tomorrow the plot begins in earnest, and the watching will be tested in a garden.

title: One of You Will Betray Me
subtitle: Mark 14:1–31
description: A jar of nard broken open, Judas gone to the priests, a last Passover, and a rooster prophesied before midnight.
paragraphs: Two days before Passover the plot finds its timetable: the chief priests and scribes want Jesus arrested by stealth and killed. “But not during the feast,” they said, “or there may be a riot among the people.” That same evening, in Bethany, at the table of Simon the Leper, a woman does the thing this Gospel will be remembered for until the end of the world. She carries an alabaster jar of pure nard worth more than three hundred denarii, breaks it open, and pours it out on his head. Some at the table scold her for the waste; the money could have fed the poor. Jesus defends her in words that reach forward to his grave: “Leave her alone; why are you bothering her? She has done a beautiful deed to Me.” “The poor you will always have with you, and you can help them whenever you want. But you will not always have Me.” “She has done what she could to anoint My body in advance of My burial.” And then the promise that has kept her anonymous act famous for two thousand years: “wherever the gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.”

The next scene is her opposite. “Then Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests to betray Jesus to them.” They are delighted, they promise money, and Judas begins watching for his opportunity. Mark gives him no speech, no grievance, no price named. The anointing and the betrayal stand back to back with nothing between them, extravagant love and quiet treachery, and the Gospel lets the contrast do the accusing. On the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples prepare the Passover in a borrowed upper room, found exactly as Jesus described, down to the man carrying a jug of water through the city streets.

At the table, in the middle of the meal, he names what is in the room: “Truly I tell you, one of you who is eating with Me will betray Me.” Grief goes around the table one by one in the form of a question: “Surely not I?” His answer narrows it to the intimacy itself: one of the Twelve, the one dipping his hand in the same bowl. Scripture and woe stand in the same breath: “The Son of Man will go just as it is written about Him, but woe to that man by whom He is betrayed! It would be better for him if he had not been born.” Then, with the betrayer still at the table, he takes bread, blesses, breaks, and gives, saying, “Take it; this is My body.” The cup goes around to all of them: “This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.” And over the last cup he makes a vow that turns the meal toward a future table: “Truly I tell you, I will no longer drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it anew in the kingdom of God.” They sing a hymn and go out into the night.

On the Mount of Olives he tells them what the night will do to all of them, not only to Judas: “You will all fall away, for it is written: ‘I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’” And in the same breath, the appointment on the far side of the falling: “But after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.” Peter will not hear of falling: “Even if all fall away, I never will.” The answer is specific to the hour and the bird: “Truly I tell you,” Jesus replied, “this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times.” Peter insists the louder: “Even if I have to die with You, I will never deny You.” And all the others said the same thing. Mark leaves them there, unanimous, confident, and hours from flight.

title: My Soul Is Overwhelmed with Sorrow
subtitle: Mark 14:32–72
description: Gethsemane's prayer, three sleepers, a kiss in the garden, a silent prisoner who finally says I am, and Peter weeping in a courtyard.
paragraphs: Gethsemane is where the Gospel's pace finally stops running and kneels. Jesus takes Peter, James, and John further in, and Mark says he “began to be deeply troubled and distressed,” and says it in his own words to the three: “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death. Stay here and keep watch.” A little farther on he falls to the ground and prays that the hour might pass from him, and the prayer is the most intimate and the most surrendered in the Bible in the same sentence: “Abba, Father,” He said, “all things are possible for You. Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will.” Abba is the family name for God, and he uses it at the moment of asking to be spared, and then hands the asking back. The cup stays.

He returns to find the three asleep, and the rebuke is aimed at the strongest of them by his old name: “Simon, are you asleep?” He asked. “Were you not able to keep watch for one hour? Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.” He goes back and prays the same prayer. He returns and finds them sleeping again, eyes heavy, with nothing to say for themselves. The third time, the watching is over: “Are you still sleeping and resting? That is enough! The hour has come. Look, the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.” Rise, let us go. The betrayer is already in the garden with torches.

Judas comes with a crowd armed with swords and clubs and uses the arranged sign, a kiss, going straight to him with a disciple's greeting on his lips. They seize Jesus, and one bystander slashes off the ear of the high priest's servant, the only blow struck by his side all night. Jesus addresses the arresting party like a man pointing out an absurdity: “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest Me as you would an outlaw? Every day I was with you, teaching in the temple courts, and you did not arrest Me. But this has happened that the Scriptures would be fulfilled.” Then the scattering he predicted arrives in six words: “Then everyone deserted Him and fled.” Mark alone preserves the strange footnote: a young man following in nothing but a linen cloth is grabbed, wrenches free of the cloth, and runs off naked into the night. The last follower to leave the garden leaves his clothes in their hands.

Inside the high priest's house the Sanhedrin hunts for testimony that will hold together and cannot find any. Witness after witness contradicts the next, even the pair who twist his temple saying into evidence: “I will destroy this man-made temple, and in three days I will build another that is made without hands.” Through all of it he is silent, until the high priest puts the identity question under oath: “Are You the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?” The silence breaks with the plainest self-naming in the Gospel: “I am,” said Jesus, “and you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.” The high priest tears his clothes, the verdict is unanimous, and the court dissolves into spitting, blindfolding, fists, and mockery: prophesy, tell us who hit you.

Below in the courtyard, warming himself at the fire, Peter meets the other trial, the small one. A servant girl looks at him: “You also were with Jesus the Nazarene.” He denies it: “I do not know or even understand what you are talking about,” and moves toward the gateway, and a rooster crows. The girl says it again to the bystanders, and he denies it again. Then the bystanders press the accent that gives him away: “Surely you are one of them, for you too are a Galilean.” This time he curses and swears his denial into an oath: “I do not know this man of whom you speak!” Immediately the rooster crows a second time, and Peter remembers the word spoken at supper, “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times,” and the man who would die with him hours ago breaks down in the courtyard and weeps.

title: Crucify Him
subtitle: Mark 15:1–47
description: Pilate's questions, Barabbas chosen, the long road to Golgotha, darkness at noon, and a centurion who says what no one else has.
paragraphs: At dawn they bind him and hand him to the Roman governor, and Pilate's whole trial turns on one title. “Are You the King of the Jews?” Jesus' answer is the last thing he says in the proceeding: “You have said so,” Jesus replied. The chief priests pour out many charges, Pilate gives him the floor again, “Have You no answer? Look how many charges they are bringing against You!” and Mark records the result: “But to Pilate’s amazement, Jesus made no further reply.” The governor can see the motive plainly enough; he knows it was envy that delivered Jesus to him. What Pilate lacks is not information. It is a spine.

The feast custom offers him an exit: release one prisoner. The crowd, steered by the chief priests, asks for Barabbas, a murderer from an insurrection, and Pilate tries once more: “What then do you want me to do with the One you call the King of the Jews?” The answer comes back as a shout, twice: “Crucify Him!” “Why?” asked Pilate. “What evil has He done?” The shout only gets louder. “And wishing to satisfy the crowd, Pilate released Barabbas to them. But he had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified.” The soldiers take over from there: a purple robe, a crown twisted from thorns, a salute in mockery, “Hail, King of the Jews!”, blows to the head with a staff, spitting, bowing. When the theater is done they put his own clothes back on him and lead him out, and when he cannot carry the cross, they conscript a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, names Mark's first readers evidently knew.

At Golgotha, the Place of the Skull, he refuses the drugged wine, and they crucify him, dividing his garments by lot underneath the cross. Mark timestamps it with a reporter's flatness: “It was the third hour when they crucified Him.” The written charge over his head is the trial's title turned into a placard: THE KING OF THE JEWS. Two robbers hang beside him, one on his right and one on his left. The passersby shake their heads and throw his own temple saying back at him. The chief priests mock among themselves, producing without knowing it the truest summary of the day: “He saved others, but He cannot save Himself!” Even the men crucified with him join the abuse. From the sixth hour to the ninth, darkness covers the land.

At the ninth hour he cries out in Aramaic, and Mark keeps the sound of it before translating: “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” It is Psalm 22 on the lips of the sufferer, and some bystanders mishear it as a call to Elijah. A sponge of sour wine is lifted on a reed. Then, with a loud cry, he breathes his last, and at that moment, across the city, “the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.” The first person in Mark to confess Jesus truly is not Peter, who said it and fled, but the Roman executioner standing in front of the cross, who watched how he died: “Truly this man was the Son of God!”

The women watch from a distance, Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James and Salome among them, women who had followed and served him since Galilee. Evening is coming, and with it the Sabbath, when no burial could be done. Into that closing window steps a member of the very council that condemned him: “Joseph of Arimathea, a prominent Council member who himself was waiting for the kingdom of God, boldly went to Pilate to ask for the body of Jesus.” He buys linen, takes the body down, wraps it, lays it in a rock-cut tomb, and rolls the stone across the entrance. And the women see where he is placed. Mark wants you to know the tomb has witnesses, because the next morning is coming.

title: They Said Nothing to Anyone
subtitle: Mark 16:1–20
description: Women at dawn, an empty tomb, a message naming Peter, the fear that ends the earliest text, and the received ending that sends the story worldwide.
paragraphs: When the Sabbath is over, three women buy spices to finish the burial properly: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome. “Very early on the first day of the week, just after sunrise, they went to the tomb,” worrying on the way about the one practical problem: “Who will roll away the stone from the entrance of the tomb?” The stone is extremely large, and they have brought no one to move it. They look up, and it has already been rolled away. Inside, where the body should be, sits a young man in a white robe, on the right side, and the women are alarmed before he says a word.

His message is the Gospel's whole news in three sentences: “Do not be alarmed. You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has risen! He is not here! See the place where they put Him.” Then the errand, with one name lifted out of the group for special mention, the name that needed it most: go, “tell His disciples and Peter, ‘He is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see Him, just as He told you.’” And Peter. The denier is named separately in the resurrection's first announcement, as if heaven is making sure the invitation reaches the one man who would assume it was not for him. The women run from the tomb trembling and bewildered, and Mark's earliest text ends in their silence: in their fear, “they did not say a word to anyone.”

Here the seam in Mark must be named plainly, because this Gospel, of all of them, refuses to end tidy. The earliest copies of Mark close at that silence, verse 8, with the tomb empty, the message delivered, and the witnesses too frightened to speak. What follows, verses 9 through 20, is the ending the church received and kept, the ending the Berean Standard Bible prints, and it is told here as it stands, on its own terms, not blended with the resurrection accounts of Matthew or Luke.

In that received ending, the risen Jesus appears first to Mary Magdalene, “from whom He had driven out seven demons,” and she carries the news to the mourners. “And when they heard that Jesus was alive and she had seen Him, they did not believe it.” He appears “in a different form” to two of them walking in the country, and their report is disbelieved too. Only when he appears to the Eleven themselves at the table does the pattern break, and it breaks with a rebuke: he upbraids them “for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen Him after He had risen.” Mark's Gospel ends with its heroes scolded for the same hard heart it diagnosed in chapter 8, and commissioned anyway.

The commission is as wide as the world: “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature.” Signs will follow those who believe, he tells them: demons driven out in his name, new tongues, serpents taken up, poison unharmed, the sick made well under their hands. And then the last picture of Jesus in Mark is a seated one: “He was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God,” the right hand of Power he had promised the council they would see. The final verse hands the story to the church: “And they went out and preached everywhere, and the Lord worked through them, confirming His word by the signs that accompanied it.” The women who said nothing are preaching everywhere by the last line. Mark ends where he began, with the gospel on the move.
